title: Type 1 Diabetes: Build the Insulin Regimen Around Physiology
bottomLine: Type 1 diabetes is absolute insulin deficiency. A safe regimen supplies basal insulin continuously and meal/correction insulin matched to carbohydrate intake, glucose trend, activity and individual sensitivity; fasting or illness may change doses but does not erase the need for basal insulin.
recognize: Basal insulin suppresses hepatic glucose/ketone production between meals and overnight; prandial insulin covers carbohydrate intake; correction insulin addresses hyperglycemia outside expected targets.
Pump users have no long-acting depot, so interruption can cause rapid insulin deficiency and DKA risk.
differentiate: Prandial insulin can be reduced/held when a meal is missed, while basal insulin in type 1 diabetes generally must continue in an adjusted form.
Persistent hyperglycemia from missed insulin differs from transient post-meal spikes and should trigger ketone/illness assessment when significant.
assessment: Review CGM/SMBG patterns, hypoglycemia, carbohydrate ratios, correction factors, injection/pump technique, site rotation, activity, illness, pregnancy and psychosocial burden.
Ask about access to insulin, glucagon, ketone testing and backup supplies.
workup: Use A1C plus CGM/time-in-range metrics or SMBG patterns to assess control; use ketone testing during illness or significant hyperglycemia when DKA risk is plausible.
management: Use individualized basal-bolus injection or pump/automated insulin delivery when appropriate.
Adjust basal from fasting/overnight patterns and prandial/correction doses from meal and trend data rather than changing all components at once.
Provide a written sick-day and pump-failure backup plan.
medicationSafety: Never omit all basal insulin in type 1 diabetes solely because the patient is NPO without a clinician-directed replacement strategy.
Insulin stacking can cause delayed hypoglycemia; review active insulin and timing before repeated corrections.
Pregnancy requires tighter specialist-guided targets and rapid dose adjustment as physiology changes.
redFlags: Ketones with vomiting or acidosis symptoms
counselling: Teach the distinct jobs of basal, meal and correction insulin and ensure caregivers know rescue glucagon when appropriate.
Review driving, exercise, alcohol and illness precautions.
followUp: Reassess patterns after meaningful dose changes rather than reacting to one isolated reading.
Use interprofessional diabetes support for recurrent severe events or technology issues.
examTrap: Holding all insulin because the patient is not eating.
oneLinePearl: No food may change prandial insulin; it does not remove the physiologic need for basal insulin in type 1 diabetes.
sourceBasis: Diabetes Canada type 1 diabetes and glucose-monitoring guidance

title: Insulin Initiation and Titration: Change the Component Causing the Pattern
bottomLine: Initiate insulin when clinical severity or glycemic pattern requires it, then titrate the specific component responsible for the pattern. Basal insulin primarily targets fasting glucose; persistent post-meal hyperglycemia despite controlled fasting glucose calls for a prandial strategy rather than endless basal escalation.
recognize: Metabolic decompensation, ketosis, hyperosmolar state, marked symptomatic hyperglycemia or catabolic weight loss can justify prompt insulin rather than slow oral-drug sequencing.
Over-basalization is suggested when fasting glucose is near target but daytime/post-meal glucose remains high and basal dose escalation causes nocturnal/fasting hypoglycemia.
differentiate: Basal titration addresses fasting pattern; prandial/correction therapy addresses meal-related excursions.
A single high glucose caused by illness/steroid exposure is different from a stable chronic pattern requiring regimen redesign.
assessment: Review A1C, fasting and post-meal pattern, hypoglycemia, kidney function, eating schedule, frailty, cognitive/visual/dexterity ability, cost and injection support.
Confirm medication adherence/technique before escalating insulin.
workup: Use structured SMBG or CGM to identify the pattern that should drive titration.
Assess renal function and concurrent medications that alter insulin needs.
management: Start with an evidence-based basal strategy for many adults when insulin is needed and no immediate prandial regimen is required.
Titrate incrementally from fasting patterns using a validated protocol, then add prandial/intensification when fasting is controlled but A1C/daytime values remain above target.
De-intensify when recurrent hypoglycemia, frailty or changing goals make the regimen unsafe.
medicationSafety: Do not copy a fixed titration schedule without considering hypoglycemia, renal decline, meal inconsistency or older-adult vulnerability.
Concentrated insulin products and pens require product-specific dose/device verification to prevent dosing errors.
counselling: Teach how and when to adjust only the authorized component of the regimen, when not to self-titrate, and how to treat hypoglycemia.
followUp: Review patterns soon after initiation/titration and reassess the need for intensification or simplification.
examTrap: Increasing basal insulin indefinitely when fasting glucose is already controlled and the problem is post-meal hyperglycemia.
oneLinePearl: Titrate the insulin that matches the glucose pattern.
sourceBasis: Diabetes Canada insulin initiation and titration tools
Diabetes Canada 2024 pharmacologic glycemic management update

title: CGM Interpretation: Patterns, Time in Range, and Hypoglycemia Before Averages
bottomLine: CGM interpretation is pattern recognition. Confirm that there is enough usable sensor data, then prioritize time below range and severe variability before chasing the average; use time in range, glucose management indicator and daily overlays to identify which regimen component needs adjustment.
recognize: Time in range summarizes exposure but does not show when excursions occur; daily profile/ambulatory glucose patterns identify overnight, post-meal or activity-related problems.
A low average can hide dangerous recurrent hypoglycemia.
differentiate: Sensor glucose lags blood glucose during rapid change; confirm with capillary glucose when symptoms do not match the sensor or device guidance recommends confirmation.
Compression lows, sensor failure and newly inserted sensors can create misleading data.
assessment: Review percent sensor wear, time below/in/above range, overnight pattern, meal/activity timing, insulin timing, illness and hypoglycemia awareness.
Ask what clinical decision the CGM pattern is meant to inform.
workup: Use AGP/time-in-range metrics with A1C and clinical context; do not diagnose DKA or severe hypoglycemia from a single sensor value without clinical confirmation when appropriate.
management: Correct recurrent hypoglycemia first, then address the dominant hyperglycemic pattern.
Change one major regimen component at a time when possible so the effect can be interpreted.
Use automated insulin-delivery features according to device-specific training rather than overriding algorithms reflexively.
medicationSafety: Avoid insulin stacking based on rapidly changing sensor values without accounting for insulin-on-board.
Pregnancy and frailty use different target/risk frameworks; standard adult targets should not be applied automatically.
redFlags: Device failure in pump-dependent type 1 diabetes
counselling: Teach trend arrows as context rather than an automatic dose command and review when fingerstick confirmation is required.
Explain that time-in-range improvement is useful even before A1C changes.
followUp: Compare standardized reports over time after therapy changes and link changes to specific outcomes.
examTrap: Adjusting insulin from one CGM spike while ignoring repeated overnight hypoglycemia.
oneLinePearl: In CGM review, prevent lows first, then fix the recurring highs.
sourceBasis: Diabetes Canada automated insulin delivery/type 1 guidance

title: HHS: Hyperosmolar Dehydration Is the Emergency
bottomLine: Hyperosmolar hyperglycemic state is a profound dehydration/hyperosmolality emergency, usually with severe hyperglycemia and less prominent ketoacidosis than DKA. Restore circulation carefully, monitor sodium/potassium/osmolality and mental status closely, use insulin after initial fluid/potassium assessment, and find the precipitant.
recognize: Marked dehydration, weakness, neurologic change and very high glucose/osmolality are typical; older adults may present with delirium or falls.
Infection, missed therapy, MI/stroke and medications are common precipitants.
differentiate: DKA is defined by ketosis/acidosis and can occur at lower glucose, especially with SGLT2 inhibitors.
HHS can coexist with DKA, so acid-base/ketone data still matter.
assessment: Assess ABCs, perfusion, mental status, volume depletion, infection/ischemia and medication access/adherence.
Look for heart/renal failure that changes fluid strategy.
workup: Obtain glucose, electrolytes, creatinine, ketones, acid-base data and calculated/effective osmolality with cause-directed testing.
Monitor corrected sodium/osmolality trends during treatment.
management: Use protocolized isotonic fluid resuscitation with repeated hemodynamic and biochemical reassessment.
Address potassium before/while giving insulin and avoid overly rapid osmotic shifts.
Treat infection/ischemia or other precipitant and continue until hyperosmolality/mental status and metabolic abnormalities resolve—not merely until glucose falls.
medicationSafety: Insulin can worsen hypokalemia and should not be started blindly in severe potassium depletion.
Aggressive fluids can harm patients with heart/renal failure; reassessment is mandatory.
counselling: After recovery, address medication access, hydration/illness planning and early symptoms of decompensation.
followUp: Ensure precipitant resolution and diabetes follow-up before discharge.
examTrap: Stopping treatment once glucose improves while hyperosmolality and neurologic dysfunction persist.
oneLinePearl: HHS is an osmolality and dehydration emergency, not just an extremely high glucose.

title: Thyroid Cancer Follow-Up: Surveillance by Recurrence Risk and Response
bottomLine: Differentiated thyroid-cancer follow-up is risk-adapted. Surveillance integrates pathology/stage, treatment history, thyroglobulin/antibody trends when applicable, neck ultrasound and the patient's evolving response category; TSH suppression intensity is individualized because benefit and harm change with recurrence risk and time.
recognize: Persistent/recurrent disease may present as rising tumor-marker trend, suspicious cervical nodes/lesions or structural disease on imaging.
Anti-thyroglobulin antibodies can interfere with thyroglobulin interpretation and their trend becomes clinically relevant.
differentiate: A detectable thyroglobulin after total thyroidectomy/ablation means something different from thyroglobulin in a patient with residual normal thyroid tissue.
Medullary thyroid cancer uses different tumor markers and surveillance than differentiated thyroid cancer.
assessment: Review histology, stage/risk, surgery/radioiodine history, current levothyroxine/TSH target, pregnancy plans and prior imaging/marker trajectory.
Examine neck and ask about voice change, dysphagia, neck mass and systemic symptoms.
workup: Use TSH, tumor-marker/antibody trends and neck ultrasound according to cancer type/risk and specialist plan.
Additional cross-sectional/nuclear imaging is selected when biochemical or structural concern warrants it rather than ordered routinely.
management: Maintain individualized levothyroxine/TSH target and coordinate endocrinology/oncology surveillance.
Escalate suspicious structural or biochemical recurrence for specialist imaging/biopsy/treatment planning.
medicationSafety: Excessive TSH suppression can increase atrial fibrillation and bone risk; it should not remain maximally suppressed indefinitely in every survivor.
Pregnancy changes thyroid-hormone requirements and surveillance planning.
redFlags: Marked biochemical rise with suspicious imaging
counselling: Explain why follow-up intensity decreases or increases according to recurrence risk/response rather than a one-size schedule.
followUp: Ensure responsibility for surveillance is explicit across primary care, endocrinology and oncology.
examTrap: Keeping every low-risk thyroid-cancer survivor on aggressive lifelong TSH suppression without reassessing benefit versus harm.
oneLinePearl: Thyroid-cancer surveillance follows recurrence risk and response—not the calendar alone.

title: Pheochromocytoma: Biochemical Diagnosis Before Localization
bottomLine: Suspect pheochromocytoma/paraganglioma when episodic or resistant hypertension occurs with adrenergic symptoms, an adrenal mass has compatible features, or hereditary risk is present. Establish catecholamine excess biochemically under appropriate sampling conditions before localization imaging whenever clinically feasible, and never start beta blockade before adequate alpha blockade in confirmed functional disease.
recognize: Paroxysmal headache, palpitations, sweating and labile hypertension are classic but not universal.
Incidental adrenal mass, young hypertension or hereditary syndromes can be the clue.
differentiate: Panic attacks, hyperthyroidism, stimulant use and medication withdrawal can mimic adrenergic spells.
A nonfunctioning adrenal incidentaloma does not become pheochromocytoma from imaging alone.
assessment: Document spell pattern, BP, medications/substances, family history/genetic syndromes and adrenal-mass history.
Ask pregnancy status because diagnosis and perioperative management become high risk.
workup: Use plasma free or urinary fractionated metanephrine testing with attention to pre-analytic conditions and interfering drugs.
After biochemical evidence, use appropriate CT/MRI and specialty-directed functional/genetic testing.
management: Refer confirmed/suspected functional disease to endocrinology/surgical specialty care.
Preoperative preparation uses alpha blockade, salt/volume planning and then beta blockade only if needed after alpha blockade.
Treat hypertensive crisis in monitored acute care with expert input.
medicationSafety: Unopposed beta blockade can precipitate dangerous vasoconstriction/hypertension in functional pheochromocytoma.
Several drugs/foods/stressors can affect biochemical testing and symptoms; verify testing instructions.
counselling: Explain why biochemical confirmation generally comes before tumor localization and why medication sequencing matters.
followUp: Coordinate genetic evaluation and long-term recurrence/surveillance plan where indicated.
examTrap: Starting a beta blocker first for tachycardia in confirmed pheochromocytoma without alpha blockade.
oneLinePearl: Prove catecholamine excess, then localize—and alpha comes before beta.

title: Hypoparathyroidism: Correct Symptoms Without Creating Hypercalciuria
bottomLine: Chronic hypoparathyroidism is low/inappropriately normal PTH with hypocalcemia after other causes are considered. Treat symptomatic/severe hypocalcemia urgently; chronic therapy aims for symptom control with low-normal calcium while avoiding hypercalciuria, renal complications and excess calcium/vitamin-D exposure.
recognize: Perioral/hand paresthesia, cramps, tetany, seizures and QT prolongation can accompany hypocalcemia.
Post-thyroid/parathyroid surgery is a common acquired cause.
differentiate: Vitamin-D deficiency, CKD, magnesium deficiency and other causes of hypocalcemia can produce different PTH patterns.
Severe hypomagnesemia can impair PTH secretion/action and make calcium difficult to correct.
assessment: Assess neuromuscular symptoms, seizures, medication/supplement use, surgery history, renal stones and pregnancy.
workup: Confirm corrected/ionized calcium as appropriate, phosphate, magnesium, creatinine/eGFR, PTH and vitamin-D context.
Monitor urinary calcium/renal complications during chronic therapy according to specialty guidance.
management: Severe symptomatic hypocalcemia requires monitored IV calcium and correction of magnesium/precipitants.
Chronic care uses oral calcium and active vitamin-D therapy individualized to symptoms, calcium/phosphate and renal risk; selected refractory patients may need specialist PTH-replacement strategies.
medicationSafety: Overtreatment can cause hypercalciuria, nephrolithiasis/nephrocalcinosis and kidney injury even when serum calcium looks acceptable.
Separate calcium from medications whose absorption it impairs when relevant.
counselling: Teach symptoms of both low and high calcium and why renal/urine monitoring matters.
followUp: Trend calcium, phosphate, magnesium, renal function and urinary calcium as clinically indicated.
examTrap: Chasing a high-normal serum calcium with escalating supplements while ignoring hypercalciuria/renal injury.
oneLinePearl: In hypoparathyroidism, the goal is symptom control without overloading the kidneys with calcium.

title: Vitamin D Deficiency: Test When the Result Will Change Care
bottomLine: Do not screen every healthy adult for vitamin-D deficiency. Test when risk, symptoms or bone/mineral disease make the result clinically actionable, then treat deficiency with an evidence-based replacement plan while avoiding megadose toxicity and investigating malabsorption/renal or other contributors when response is poor.
recognize: Low intake/sun exposure alone does not always require testing; osteomalacia, malabsorption, CKD, anticonvulsant exposure and severe osteoporosis can make assessment more useful.
Severe deficiency can contribute to bone pain, proximal weakness and secondary hyperparathyroidism.
differentiate: Osteoporosis is not synonymous with vitamin-D deficiency; osteomalacia is a mineralization disorder with different biochemical clues.
Low total calcium from hypoalbuminemia should not be misread as true hypocalcemia without context.
assessment: Review fracture/bone pain, diet, supplements, malabsorption/bariatric surgery, kidney/liver disease, medications and pregnancy.
workup: Use 25-hydroxyvitamin D when testing is indicated and interpret with calcium, phosphate, ALP/PTH/renal data when metabolic bone disease is suspected.
Avoid routine repeated testing after standard supplementation unless the result will change management.
management: Use oral vitamin-D replacement appropriate to severity/risk and ensure adequate calcium intake primarily through diet when possible.
Investigate adherence, malabsorption or renal/metabolic disease if deficiency does not respond as expected.
medicationSafety: Excess chronic vitamin D can cause hypercalcemia/hypercalciuria and kidney injury; avoid unregulated high-dose regimens.
Granulomatous disease can increase active vitamin-D production and changes supplementation risk.
counselling: Explain that more vitamin D is not always better and that supplements should be matched to actual risk/need.
followUp: Recheck when severe deficiency, malabsorption or an ongoing high-risk state makes confirmation useful.
examTrap: Ordering routine vitamin-D levels annually in every healthy adult or prescribing chronic megadoses without monitoring risk.
oneLinePearl: Test vitamin D when the answer changes care; treat deficiency without creating toxicity.

title: Metabolic Bone Disease: Fracture Risk Is Not the Whole Differential
bottomLine: When fractures, bone pain or abnormal mineral labs do not fit routine osteoporosis, broaden to metabolic bone disease. Distinguish osteoporosis from osteomalacia, hyper/hypoparathyroidism, CKD-mineral bone disorder and other secondary causes before choosing antiresorptive therapy.
recognize: Fragility fracture/low BMD can result from osteoporosis, but bone pain, proximal weakness or abnormal calcium/phosphate/ALP can suggest another mineralization disorder.
Younger age, multiple fractures or unexpectedly severe disease increases the likelihood of secondary causes.
differentiate: Osteoporosis has normal mineralization; osteomalacia is defective mineralization and often has biochemical abnormalities.
CKD alters PTH/phosphate/vitamin-D physiology and requires a CKD-MBD framework rather than ordinary osteoporosis treatment alone.
assessment: Review fracture history, nutrition, GI/malabsorption, renal disease, steroids/antiepileptics, endocrine disease, menstrual/hypogonadal history and family history.
Assess height loss, kyphosis, bone tenderness and proximal strength.
workup: Use calcium, phosphate, ALP, renal function, PTH/vitamin-D and other targeted testing according to phenotype.
Use DXA/fracture-risk assessment where osteoporosis is part of the question but do not let BMD replace secondary-cause evaluation.
management: Treat the underlying mineral/endocrine/renal disorder and correct nutrient deficiency before or alongside fracture-prevention therapy.
Refer unusual, severe, young-onset or diagnostically unclear metabolic bone disease to endocrinology/metabolic bone specialty care.
medicationSafety: Bisphosphonate/denosumab treatment should not be started reflexively when osteomalacia or severe mineral abnormality is untreated.
Renal function and calcium/vitamin-D status influence antiresorptive safety.
redFlags: Multiple unexplained fractures in a young patient
counselling: Explain that low bone strength can arise from different mechanisms and treatment depends on which process is present.
followUp: Track cause-specific biochemical response and fracture risk rather than repeating DXA too frequently.
examTrap: Treating low BMD as osteoporosis without recognizing osteomalacia or CKD-mineral bone disease.
oneLinePearl: Low BMD is a finding; metabolic bone diagnosis still requires mechanism.

title: Pituitary Adenoma: Hormone Excess, Hormone Failure, or Mass Effect?
bottomLine: A pituitary adenoma is evaluated on three axes: hormone hypersecretion, pituitary hormone deficiency and mass effect. New visual-field loss or pituitary apoplexy symptoms are emergencies; otherwise, targeted endocrine testing precedes treatment and management depends on tumor type/size and symptoms.
recognize: Headache/visual-field loss can reflect mass effect; amenorrhea/galactorrhea, acromegalic features or Cushing phenotype can signal hormone excess.
Large lesions can cause central hypothyroidism, adrenal insufficiency or hypogonadism.
differentiate: Mild prolactin elevation may come from stalk effect or medications rather than a prolactinoma.
Central hypothyroidism can have low free T4 with an inappropriately normal/low TSH; TSH alone can be misleading.
assessment: Assess vision, headache, menstrual/sexual function, galactorrhea, growth/acromegaly/Cushing features and symptoms of adrenal/thyroid deficiency.
workup: Obtain targeted prolactin, IGF-1, cortisol-axis and thyroid/gonadal testing according to phenotype and MRI pituitary when indicated.
Formal visual-field testing is required when the lesion approaches/compresses the optic apparatus.
management: Prolactinomas are usually treated medically with dopamine agonist therapy; other functioning or compressive tumors often require endocrine/neurosurgical planning.
Replace deficient hormones safely, ensuring adrenal insufficiency is addressed before starting thyroid hormone when both are possible.
medicationSafety: Starting levothyroxine before treating unrecognized central adrenal insufficiency can precipitate adrenal crisis.
Dopamine agonists require monitoring for orthostasis, nausea and rare behavioral effects.
redFlags: Sudden severe headache with visual loss/ophthalmoplegia
counselling: Explain the difference between hormone function and tumor size; both determine treatment.
followUp: Track hormone levels, visual fields and MRI according to tumor type/risk and treatment response.
examTrap: Treating central hypothyroidism with levothyroxine before excluding/treating central adrenal insufficiency.
oneLinePearl: Pituitary adenoma care asks: what is it secreting, what is it suppressing, and what is it compressing?
